title: Hybrid Fuzzing with LLM-Guided Input Mutation and Semantic Feedback
authors: Shiyin Lin
abstract: Software fuzzing has become a cornerstone in automated vulnerability discovery, yet existing mutation strategies often lack semantic awareness, leading to redundant test cases and slow exploration of deep program states. In this work, we present a hybrid fuzzing framework that integrates static and dynamic analysis with Large Language Model (LLM)-guided input mutation and semantic feedback. Static analysis extracts control-flow and data-flow information, which is transformed into structured prompts for the LLM to generate syntactically valid and semantically diverse inputs. During execution, we augment traditional coverage-based feedback with semantic feedback signals—derived from program state changes, exception types, and output semantics—allowing the fuzzer to prioritize inputs that trigger novel program behaviors beyond mere code coverage. We implement our approach atop AFL++, combining program instrumentation with embedding-based semantic similarity metrics to guide seed selection. Evaluation on real-world open-source targets, including libpng, tcpdump, and sqlite, demonstrates that our method achieves faster time-to-first-bug, higher semantic diversity, and a competitive number of unique bugs compared to state-of-the-art fuzzers. This work highlights the potential of combining LLM reasoning with semantic-aware feedback to accelerate and deepen vulnerability discovery.

title: Improve Model Testing by Integrating Bounded Model Checking and Coverage Guided Fuzzing
authors: yixiao yang
abstract: Abstract           The control logic models built by Simulink or Ptolemy have been widely used in industry scenes. It is an urgent need to ensure the safety and security of the control logic models. Test case generation technologies are widely used to ensure the safety and security. State-of-the-art model testing tools employ model checking techniques or search-based methods to generate test cases. Traditional search based techniques based on Simulink simulation are plagued by problems such as low speed and high overhead. Traditional model checking techniques such as symbolic execution have limited performance when dealing with nonlinear elements and complex loops. Recently, coverage guided fuzzing technologies are known to be effective for test case generation, due to their high efficiency and impressive effects over complex branches of loops. In this paper, we apply fuzzing methods to improve model testing and demonstrate the effectiveness. The fuzzing methods aim to cover more program branches by mutating valuable seeds. Inspired by this feature, we propose a novel integration technology SPsCGF, which leverages bounded model checking for symbolic execution to generate test cases as initial seeds and then conduct fuzzing based upon these worthy seeds. In this manner, our work combines the advantages of the model checking methods and fuzzing techniques in a novel way. Over the evaluated benchmarks which consist of industrial cases, SPsCGF could achieve 8% to 38% higher model coverage and 3x-10x time efficiency compared with the state-of-the-art works.

title: LLM-Guided Semantic Mutation for Lua Interpreter Fuzzing: A Coverage-Driven Approach
authors: Richard Facin Souza; Andrei de Almeida Sampaio Braga; Samuel da Silva Feitosa; Giancarlo Dondoni Salton
venue: Anais do XXX Simpósio Brasileiro de Linguagens de Programação (SBLP 2026)
abstract: Fuzzing is a crucial technique for finding vulnerabilities in software, but its effectiveness in scripting languages such as Lua is limited by the difficulty of generating semantically valid test inputs. This work proposes a methodology that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate semantically rich mutations for fuzzing Lua scripts. Our approach involves developing a fuzzer prototype that leverages an LLM’s in-context learning capabilities to create syntactically and semantically plausible code variations. We will validate this methodology by evaluating the code coverage gain of mutations relative to original seeds, the effectiveness in bug identification, and the execution time of the process, aiming to demonstrate the feasibility of using LLMs for the security of systems utilizing Lua.

title: KubeAPIFuzzer: Achieving State-aware and Coverage-guided Fuzzing for Kubernetes RESTful APIs
authors: Chen Wang; Hongbo Tang; Zichen Zhao; Yu Zhao; Hang Qiu
abstract: Kubernetes has become a de facto orchestration platform for cloud-native infrastructure and AI workloads. It uses RESTful APIs that allow users and external systems to communicate with Kubernetes clusters and components. However, these exposed API interfaces introduce reliability and security risks. Existing RESTful API fuzzers mainly rely on OpenAPI specifications and black-box request generation. They, therefore, struggle to capture Kubernetes-specific resource semantics, maintain runtime state dependencies, and obtain effective coverage feedback from Go-based Kubernetes components. Consequently, systematic fuzzing techniques tailored to Kubernetes RESTful APIs remain largely underexplored. This paper presents KubeAPIFuzzer, a state-aware and coverage-guided fuzzing framework for Kubernetes RESTful APIs. KubeAPIFuzzer introduces three techniques: semantic-aware initial seed construction, state-aware request mutation, and Go platform coverage feedback. The first constructs initial requests according to resource lifecycle ordering and Kubernetes-specific field semantics, and refines invalid requests using field-level information in error responses. The second extracts runtime state values from successful responses and reuses them to guide later mutations. The third emits coverage snapshots after API request processing and compares adjacent snapshots to retain high-value seeds for deep path exploration.We implement KubeAPIFuzzer and evaluate it on two recent Kubernetes releases, 1.33.1 and 1.36.0. Compared with the strongest baselines, KubeAPIFuzzer achieves higher request validity and improves average statement coverage by 9.1--9.7 percentage points. It identifies 20 representative bug-triggering cases, grouped into 10 distinct bug patterns. We reported the related issues and patches to the Kubernetes community, and six have been confirmed.
